segments.heading: Abstract
segments.text: We present a fatal case of amoebic encephalitis due to Acanthamoeba spp. in an immunosuppressed male. Amoebic encephalitis can be a diagnostic challenge as clinical features are non-specific and imaging findings resemble other more common diagnoses such as tumours, haemorrhage or encephalitis from other causes. Here, we present the diagnostic imaging findings in this case and review the reported imaging findings in other cases throughout the literature.

segments.heading: Clinical presentation
segments.text: 52-year-old immunosuppressed male presented with fever, impaired consciousness and headache. Past medical history comprised curatively resected gastric cancer (T1N0M0) complicated by post-operative pancytopenia and diagnosis of aplastic anaemia on bone marrow biopsy. Subsequent bone marrow transplantation led to graft versus host disease and, at the time of presentation, the patient had pancytopenia and was being treated with prednisolone.

segments.heading: Investigations/imaging findings
segments.text: CT scan of the chest (Figure 1) revealed a dense mass consolidation with surrounding ground-glass opacity in the right upper lobe. Staphylococcus was identified from blood cultures and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia from bronchiolar lavage, but pathological examination of the cerebrospinal fluid was unremarkable. Serial CT brain investigations (Figure 2) performed 2 days apart demonstrated a rapidly growing low density mass in the left parietal lobe.

segments.heading: Investigations/imaging findings
segments.text: 3.0 T MRI brain (Figure 3) was performed without contrast owing to gadolinium and iodine allergies. T_(1) weighted images revealed a large 50 mm pseudotumoral low signal dense area in the left parietal lobe with patchy central high signal, and a separate 33 mm low signal dense homogeneous area in the left occipital lobe. On T_(2) weighted images, the two masses were seen with a central area of high signal, low signal rim and surrounding oedema. T_(2) gradient echo images revealed stronger central low signal areas, indicating haemorrhagic change. Fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) images demonstrated hyperintense lesions and there was restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging.

segments.heading: Differential diagnoses
segments.text: Infective encephalitis—considered the primary differential.

segments.heading: Differential diagnoses
segments.text: Tumour (primary or secondary from previous gastric cancer).

segments.heading: Differential diagnoses
segments.text: Infarction—considered less likely as the cerebral cortex was preserved.

segments.heading: Differential diagnoses
segments.text: Post-transplantation lymphoproliferative disease.

segments.heading: Differential diagnoses
segments.text: Tumefactive demyelination.

segments.heading: Treatment and outcome
segments.text: The patient developed multiorganism septicaemia, with the pathogens identified including Cryptococcus, Nocardia and Staphylococcal species. A broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen was commenced comprising doripenem, linezolid, clindamycin and azithromycin, but the patient’s condition deteriorated further and he required intubation. Decompressive neurosurgery for cerebral oedema was carried out but unfortunately the patient died. Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis due to Acanthamoeba spp. was diagnosed on autopsy, with ameobic lesions also found in the lungs.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Four free-living amoebae species have been reported to cause encephalitis in humans: Acanthamoeba spp., Balamuthia mandrillaris, Naegleria fowleri and Sappinia diploidea. Amoebic encephalitis typically affects only immunocompromised patients,^(,) although it can occur in immunocompetent healthy individuals, particularly from N. fowleri. The high proportion (38%) of healthy individuals in reviewed cases almost certainly reflects a tendency to publish rarer cases in the literature rather than the true proportion of immunocompetent patients affected. Amoebic encephalitis has a mortality rate of over 90% with no established effective treatments, although there may be some potential options for certain organisms,^(–) and is often a post-mortem pathological diagnosis.^(,) Imaging diagnosis is difficult, but our review of the findings in published case reports revealed some “typical” features such as hypointensity on T_(1 )weighted MRI, hyperintensity on T_(2 )weighted MRI, contrast enhancement, haemorrhage, oedema and mass effects, but these are not definitive and were not observed in all cases. Furthermore, differential diagnoses such as encephalitis from a different pathogen (viral, bacterial, etc.) tumour (primary or secondary) and infarction also exhibit many of these imaging features. Sound knowledge of the spectrum of imaging findings in amoebic encephalitis is essential for facilitating early accurate diagnosis and providing the patient with the best chance of survival.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: From the limited understanding of this rare diagnosis, our case report represents a fairly typical history and series of imaging findings in amoebic encephalitis, including hypointensity on T_(1) and hyperintensity on T_(2). Contrast enhancement was reported in 75% of cases and was the most consistent finding; however, there were four cases (14%) where contrast was used but the amoebic lesion(s) did not enhance. Haemorrhage on CT, gradient echo or other MRI sequences has also proven to be a particularly common feature, with several authors, including LaFleur et al (2013), commenting on central low signal on T_(2) images to suspect central haemorrhage. Too few cases have described the appearance of haemorrhage on FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging, meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarction or necrosis to estimate its frequency in amoebic encephalitis, but there may be valuable additional diagnostic findings such as hyperintensity on FLAIR, restricted diffusion and meningeal enhancement.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: The case series by Singh et al suggests that there may be variation in imaging findings, depending on the causative organism. The five cases presented had different causative organisms and significant points of difference in their radiological appearance, including density on CT scan and intensity on MRI, but all demonstrated contrast enhancement. Another case series by Galarza et al reported four paediatric cases of amoebic encephalitis, all with B. mandrillaris as the causative organism, with more consistent imaging findings. All four cases were described as hypodense on CT scan and hyperintense on T_(2) MRI, with some variation in T_(1) intensity and contrast uptake.

All four cases were described as hypodense on CT scan and hyperintense on T2 MRI, with some variation in T1 intensity and contrast uptake.

segments.heading: Conclusions
segments.text: This case demonstrates the clinical presentation, diagnostic uncertainty and fatal outcome typical for the rare disease ameobic encephalitis. The imaging findings in this case and throughout the literature demonstrated that there are several common cerebral imaging findings, but they are inconsistent and may vary depending on the causative organism. From a diagnostic imaging perspective, it is important to have a high level of clinical suspicion of amoebic encephalitis when faced with intracranial mass lesions in an immunocompromised patient.

segments.heading: Learning Points
segments.text: Amoebic encephalitis is a rare, usually fatal infective disease that generally affects immunocompromised patients.

segments.heading: Learning Points
segments.text: Common findings on cerebral imaging are hypodense mass lesion(s) on CT scan, hypointensity on T_(1) MRI, hyperintensity on T_(2) MRI, contrast enhancement (may be ring or peripheral), haemorrhage, oedema and mass effects. Additional findings may include hyperintensity on FLAIR images, restricted diffusion and meningeal enhancement.

segments.heading: Learning Points
segments.text: The “typical” imaging findings are not observed in all cases of amoebic encephalitis and there may be variation depending on the causative organism.

segments.heading: Learning Points
segments.text: Diagnostic radiologists must have a high level of suspicion of amoebic encephalitis when faced with intracranial mass lesions in a patient with immunosuppression.

segments.heading: Consent
segments.text: The patient presented in the case report is deceased, but the next of kin has provided consent for publication of the case report and images.

[b00001] Abstract
We present a fatal case of amoebic encephalitis due to Acanthamoeba spp. in an immunosuppressed male. Amoebic encephalitis can be a diagnostic challenge as clinical features are non-specific and imaging findings resemble other more common diagnoses such as tumours, haemorrhage or encephalitis from other causes. Here, we present the diagnostic imaging findings in this case and review the reported imaging findings in other cases throughout the literature.

[b00002] Clinical presentation
52-year-old immunosuppressed male presented with fever, impaired consciousness and headache. Past medical history comprised curatively resected gastric cancer (T1N0M0) complicated by post-operative pancytopenia and diagnosis of aplastic anaemia on bone marrow biopsy. Subsequent bone marrow transplantation led to graft versus host disease and, at the time of presentation, the patient had pancytopenia and was being treated with prednisolone.

[b00003] Investigations/imaging findings
CT scan of the chest (Figure 1) revealed a dense mass consolidation with surrounding ground-glass opacity in the right upper lobe. Staphylococcus was identified from blood cultures and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia from bronchiolar lavage, but pathological examination of the cerebrospinal fluid was unremarkable. Serial CT brain investigations (Figure 2) performed 2 days apart demonstrated a rapidly growing low density mass in the left parietal lobe.

[b00004] Investigations/imaging findings
3.0 T MRI brain (Figure 3) was performed without contrast owing to gadolinium and iodine allergies. T_(1) weighted images revealed a large 50 mm pseudotumoral low signal dense area in the left parietal lobe with patchy central high signal, and a separate 33 mm low signal dense homogeneous area in the left occipital lobe. On T_(2) weighted images, the two masses were seen with a central area of high signal, low signal rim and surrounding oedema. T_(2) gradient echo images revealed stronger central low signal areas, indicating haemorrhagic change. Fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) images demonstrated hyperintense lesions and there was restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging.

[b00005] Differential diagnoses
Infective encephalitis—considered the primary differential.

[b00006] Differential diagnoses
Tumour (primary or secondary from previous gastric cancer).

[b00007] Differential diagnoses
Infarction—considered less likely as the cerebral cortex was preserved.

[b00008] Differential diagnoses
Post-transplantation lymphoproliferative disease.

[b00009] Differential diagnoses
Tumefactive demyelination.

[b00010] Treatment and outcome
The patient developed multiorganism septicaemia, with the pathogens identified including Cryptococcus, Nocardia and Staphylococcal species. A broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen was commenced comprising doripenem, linezolid, clindamycin and azithromycin, but the patient’s condition deteriorated further and he required intubation. Decompressive neurosurgery for cerebral oedema was carried out but unfortunately the patient died. Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis due to Acanthamoeba spp. was diagnosed on autopsy, with ameobic lesions also found in the lungs.

Sound knowledge of the spectrum of imaging findings in amoebic encephalitis is essential for facilitating early accurate diagnosis and providing the patient with the best chance of survival.

[b00038] Discussion
From the limited understanding of this rare diagnosis, our case report represents a fairly typical history and series of imaging findings in amoebic encephalitis, including hypointensity on T_(1) and hyperintensity on T_(2). Contrast enhancement was reported in 75% of cases and was the most consistent finding; however, there were four cases (14%) where contrast was used but the amoebic lesion(s) did not enhance. Haemorrhage on CT, gradient echo or other MRI sequences has also proven to be a particularly common feature, with several authors, including LaFleur et al (2013), commenting on central low signal on T_(2) images to suspect central haemorrhage. Too few cases have described the appearance of haemorrhage on FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging, meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarction or necrosis to estimate its frequency in amoebic encephalitis, but there may be valuable additional diagnostic findings such as hyperintensity on FLAIR, restricted diffusion and meningeal enhancement.

[b00039] Discussion
The case series by Singh et al suggests that there may be variation in imaging findings, depending on the causative organism. The five cases presented had different causative organisms and significant points of difference in their radiological appearance, including density on CT scan and intensity on MRI, but all demonstrated contrast enhancement. Another case series by Galarza et al reported four paediatric cases of amoebic encephalitis, all with B. mandrillaris as the causative organism, with more consistent imaging findings. All four cases were described as hypodense on CT scan and hyperintense on T_(2) MRI, with some variation in T_(1) intensity and contrast uptake.

[b00040] Conclusions
This case demonstrates the clinical presentation, diagnostic uncertainty and fatal outcome typical for the rare disease ameobic encephalitis. The imaging findings in this case and throughout the literature demonstrated that there are several common cerebral imaging findings, but they are inconsistent and may vary depending on the causative organism. From a diagnostic imaging perspective, it is important to have a high level of clinical suspicion of amoebic encephalitis when faced with intracranial mass lesions in an immunocompromised patient.

[b00041] Learning Points
Amoebic encephalitis is a rare, usually fatal infective disease that generally affects immunocompromised patients.

[b00042] Learning Points
Common findings on cerebral imaging are hypodense mass lesion(s) on CT scan, hypointensity on T_(1) MRI, hyperintensity on T_(2) MRI, contrast enhancement (may be ring or peripheral), haemorrhage, oedema and mass effects. Additional findings may include hyperintensity on FLAIR images, restricted diffusion and meningeal enhancement.

[b00043] Learning Points
The “typical” imaging findings are not observed in all cases of amoebic encephalitis and there may be variation depending on the causative organism.

[b00044] Learning Points
Diagnostic radiologists must have a high level of suspicion of amoebic encephalitis when faced with intracranial mass lesions in a patient with immunosuppression.

[b00045] Consent
The patient presented in the case report is deceased, but the next of kin has provided consent for publication of the case report and images.
